title: Exponential Integrate-and-Fire
intro: The exponential integrate-and-fire (EIF) neuron keeps the LIF's leak but replaces its hard threshold with an exponential current that models how sodium channels start a spike.

blocks.source:
C dV/dt = -g_L (V - E_L) + g_L * Delta_T * exp( (V - V_T) / Delta_T ) + I(t)

if V >= V_peak:   V <- V_r

blocks.text: Far below V_T the exponential term is negligible and the neuron behaves like a LIF. Near V_T it grows rapidly and overwhelms the leak: the membrane potential takes off on its own, the spike upstroke. V_T is the rheobase threshold, the voltage at which the resting and unstable fixed points merge when the input reaches rheobase, and V_peak (here 20 mV) is just a numerical cutoff. Because the trajectory diverges to infinity in finite time, the exact cutoff barely matters.

Fourcaud-Trocmé and colleagues (2003) showed that the sodium current's activation near threshold is well described by an exponential. Badel and colleagues (2008) then measured the "dynamic I-V curve" of layer-5 pyramidal neurons of somatosensory cortex directly, and an exponential fitted it well, with a slope factor Delta_T of 1.2 ± 0.4 mV across 12 cells: spike initiation in these cells is sharp, sharper than in the Wang-Buzsáki conductance model. So the EIF is a fit to data, not only a convenience. (The Brette-Gerstner value of 2 mV used below is a little softer than that measured average.)

items: Delta_T (slope factor, mV): how sharp spike initiation is. As Delta_T goes to 0 the EIF becomes the LIF with threshold V_T. Larger Delta_T gives a softer threshold: spike initiation starts earlier and more gradually, and the response to rapidly changing input becomes slower.
V_T (mV): the soft threshold. A constant input must push V above roughly V_T to cause a spike.
g_L, C, E_L: as in the LIF (tau_m = C / g_L).
V_r: reset potential after a spike.

blocks.text: The I-V curve: where the threshold lives

Plot the drive dV/dt (times C) against V for zero input. Fixed points are where the curve crosses zero. The LIF line crosses once, at rest. The EIF curve bends upward, has its minimum at V_T, and crosses zero a second time a few mV above V_T: the unstable fixed point. Input current shifts the whole curve up. At rheobase the two fixed points merge and disappear (a saddle-node bifurcation), and the neuron fires repetitively. That is exactly the type I excitability seen in many cortical cells.

Compare with the LIF: the voltage now curves smoothly into each spike instead of hitting a line. Increase Delta_T and the upswing starts earlier and more gradually. These are the Brette-Gerstner constants: C = 281 pF, g_L = 30 nS, E_L = -70.6 mV, V_T = -50.4 mV.

items: When spike timing in response to fast-fluctuating input matters: the EIF's soft threshold gives realistic high-frequency response, which the LIF gets wrong.
As the base of AdEx, which adds adaptation (#/snn/neuron-models/adex).
In theory: the EIF's f-I curve and response to noise can be computed with Fokker-Planck methods (#/neuroscience/neuronal-dynamics).

blocks.text: For a cortical column: the EIF on its own lacks adaptation, so it is rarely the final choice for pyramidal cells. But it is the most accurate one-variable neuron, and if you use AdEx you are already using it: set a = b = 0 in AdEx and you have the EIF.

Sources: Fourcaud-Trocmé, Hansel, van Vreeswijk & Brunel, "How spike generation mechanisms determine the neuronal response to fluctuating inputs" (Journal of Neuroscience, 2003); Badel et al., "Dynamic I-V curves are reliable predictors of naturalistic pyramidal-neuron voltage traces" (Journal of Neurophysiology, 2008); Gerstner, Kistler, Naud & Paninski, Neuronal Dynamics (Cambridge University Press, 2014), chapter 5.
